attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, published under his name.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both his premise (hardly anyone trusts OpenAI) and his mild causal remark ('can't be great for business'). Causal kind fits.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'hardly anyone' as a very small share, plus some business harm, is ordinary and fair. The period and audience are the drafter's choices, and the contract flags them. The result turns on that reading.

evidence.note: April 2026 representative poll on Altman's favorability, not trust in OpenAI. Most respondents were unfamiliar or neutral, and views leaned negative.
May 2026 poll on trust in AI company CEOs in general. Not OpenAI-specific, though it suggests trust is low but not near zero.
Q2 2026 business results: revenue still growing, losses wider. Slowdown is attributed to competition and pricing, not distrust, so it does not test the causal link.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no OpenAI-specific trust measure and no evidence linking distrust to lost customers or revenue. The polls cover Altman or AI CEOs in general, and the business report gives other causes. The evidence neither shows that hardly anyone trusts OpenAI nor that distrust hurt its business.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post. The quoted X replies are other people's and are not part of the claim.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his 'as far as I can tell' qualifier and the target (the Aug 18 pause announcement). It is an observation about how people reacted.

contract.note: Reading it as nearly all reactions doubting the safety rationale is ordinary. 'As far as I can tell' and the undefined group are flagged, and the result depends on how the audience is defined.

evidence.note: Confirms that 'some analysts' doubted the safety rationale. Gives no measure of how widespread the doubt was.
Reports the company's safety account. That is reporting, not evidence that commentators believed it.

reviews.rationale: The only source shows skepticism existed among some analysts, but there is no sample of replies, sentiment analysis, or poll. Nothing shows whether nearly all reactions, or only some, doubted the safety rationale.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence, written right after he quotes the WSJ reporter's loss figures.

semantics.note: Although phrased generically ('you don't want'), the sentence plainly implies that OpenAI's quarterly losses quadrupled. The factual core is checkable.

contract.note: He cites the WSJ Q1-to-Q2 comparison just before this line, so quarter over quarter on operating loss is the natural reading. 'Quadruple' means about 4x, which is clear.

evidence.note: WSJ via Outlook: operating loss went from $9.3B in Q1 to $12.3B in Q2, about 1.32x.
WSJ via Enterprise: operating loss up 32% quarter over quarter, far from the 300% rise a quadrupling would need.
Independent report (via The Information) confirms the Q1 2026 operating loss of $9.3B, the base for the ratio.

reviews.rationale: Reported figures put Q2 2026 operating loss at $12.3B against $9.3B in Q1, a 32% rise (about 1.32x), not a quadrupling. A year-over-year reading cannot be checked from the packet and does not fit the quarter-over-quarter figures he cited.
